## Business question and data status

A telecommunications company wants to understand where cancellations and recurring-revenue exposure are concentrated. This teaching data set is **simulated** with a fixed random seed; monthly prices use USD solely as an illustrative unit. It contains no real customer records and must not be cited as industry evidence. The script in `data/generate_simulated_data.R` explains the rules that generated it.

## Import and inspect

`read_csv()` imports the comma-separated file and infers column types. Check the number of rows, names, types, and missing values before interpreting a summary.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

customers_raw <- read_csv("data/customer_churn_simulated.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(customers_raw)
summarise(customers_raw,
          customers = n(),
          missing_monthly_charge = sum(is.na(monthly_charge)))
```

## Clean and create analysis variables

Missing monthly charges are imputed with the median among customers on the same contract type. This preserves plan-level price differences better than one overall median. We retain and report the number imputed. Tenure is grouped into three readable bands.

```{r}
missing_charge_n <- sum(is.na(customers_raw$monthly_charge))

contract_medians <- customers_raw |>
  group_by(contract) |>
  summarise(contract_median = median(monthly_charge, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

customers <- customers_raw |>
  left_join(contract_medians, by = "contract") |>
  mutate(
    monthly_charge = if_else(is.na(monthly_charge), contract_median, monthly_charge),
    contract = factor(contract, levels = c("Month-to-month", "One year", "Two year")),
    tenure_band = cut(tenure_months, breaks = c(0, 12, 36, Inf),
                      labels = c("0–12 months", "13–36 months", "37+ months")),
    churn_flag = as.integer(churn == "Yes"),
    monthly_revenue = monthly_charge
  ) |>
  select(-contract_median)

missing_charge_n
summary(customers$monthly_charge)
```

Imputation makes the revenue summaries possible but can change group means; it does not restore unknown individual charges.

## Summarize churn by segment

A churn rate is a proportion, so the denominator is all customers in the segment. The table reports sample size alongside rate.

```{r}
contract_summary <- customers |>
  group_by(contract) |>
  summarise(
    customers = n(),
    churned = sum(churn_flag),
    churn_rate = mean(churn_flag),
    churned_mrr = sum(monthly_revenue[churn_flag == 1]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(churn_rate))

contract_summary
```

The churned MRR is the sum of monthly charges associated with observed churned accounts. It is not annual loss or a causal estimate.

## Compare tenure and contract patterns

```{r}
tenure_summary <- customers |>
  group_by(tenure_band) |>
  summarise(customers = n(), churn_rate = mean(churn_flag), .groups = "drop")

segment_summary <- customers |>
  group_by(contract, tenure_band) |>
  summarise(customers = n(), churn_rate = mean(churn_flag),
            active_mrr = sum(monthly_revenue[churn_flag == 0]),
            churned_mrr = sum(monthly_revenue[churn_flag == 1]),
            .groups = "drop")

tenure_summary
segment_summary
```

## Visualize rate and revenue exposure

```{r}
ggplot(contract_summary, aes(x = contract, y = churn_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C6E8F", width = .68) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(title = "Observed churn rate by contract type",
       x = NULL, y = "Customers marked as churned") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

A separate measure makes the financial scale visible. The scenario estimate applies each contract group's observed rate to its active monthly revenue. It is a rough prioritization device, not a forecast.

```{r}
revenue_risk <- customers |>
  group_by(contract) |>
  summarise(
    active_customers = sum(churn_flag == 0),
    observed_churn_rate = mean(churn_flag),
    active_mrr = sum(monthly_revenue[churn_flag == 0]),
    observed_churned_mrr = sum(monthly_revenue[churn_flag == 1]),
    illustrative_next_period_exposure = active_mrr * observed_churn_rate,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

revenue_risk

ggplot(revenue_risk, aes(x = contract, y = illustrative_next_period_exposure)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#B36B35", width = .68) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(prefix = "$", accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Illustrative monthly revenue exposure",
       subtitle = "Active MRR multiplied by the segment's observed churn rate",
       x = NULL, y = "Simulated USD per month") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## Interpretation and decision limits

Read the rate, group size, and currency measure together. A high churn rate in a small segment does not automatically imply the largest revenue exposure. The simulated data-generating process intentionally links churn with contract type, tenure, and support contacts, so its patterns cannot establish real-world causes.

Validate measures on a defined period of real, privacy-protected data; check whether billing and churn dates align; and investigate service issues. If the company wants to know whether an offer reduces churn, test it with a credible comparison group. Descriptive differences alone do not identify an intervention effect.
